subject: Accounting
title: The Chart of Accounts
description: One-minute skill: The Chart of Accounts.

hook.text: Every company has a master list of all its accounts—like a filing system for money.

buildup.text: The chart of accounts organizes accounts into categories: assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, expenses.

discovery.text: Each account gets a unique number—making it easy to sort, reference, and report on transactions.

twist.text: A messy chart of accounts creates confusion. A well-designed one makes reporting effortless.

climax.text: The chart is typically set up once and updated as the business grows and adds new types of transactions.

punchline.text: Organize the accounts first. Everything else follows.

quiz.question: What is a chart of accounts?
options: A master list organizing all of a company's accounts
A list of employees and their salaries

details.summary: The chart of accounts is the complete list of all account names and numbers a business uses to organize its financial transactions. This topic explains how to structure it, choose account numbers, and why a well-designed chart makes everything else in bookkeeping easier.
details.whyItMatters: The chart of accounts is the backbone of your bookkeeping system. A poorly designed chart creates confusion, miscategorized transactions, and reports that don't provide useful information.
takeaways: Accounts are typically numbered in groups: assets start at 1000, liabilities at 2000, equity at 3000
The chart should be detailed enough for useful reporting but simple enough to use consistently
Leaving gaps in numbering allows new accounts to be added without restructuring

faq.question: What is a chart of accounts?
faq.answer: A chart of accounts is a complete, organized list of every account in a company's bookkeeping system, each with a unique number and name. It categorizes all financial activity into assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, and expenses.

faq.question: How many accounts should a small business have in its chart of accounts?
faq.answer: Most small businesses need 30-50 accounts to start. The key is having enough detail for meaningful reports—separating rent from utilities, for example—without so many accounts that categorization becomes confusing and inconsistent.
